# What are the tell tale signs of a catalytic converter that might be going bad?

A failing catalytic converter often manifests itself through specific drivability symptoms rather than just a lit check engine light. The most immediate indicator is a noticeable reduction in power. As the internal substrate becomes clogged with melted catalyst material or unburnt fuel deposits, exhaust gas backpressure increases significantly. This restriction forces the engine to work harder to expel combustion gases, resulting in sluggish acceleration and a feeling of the vehicle being "flat" under load.

In the case of the 2007 Pontiac G6 you own, this power loss aligns with the specific recall campaigns issued for that model year. Some units suffered from poor manufacturing quality, while others experienced material buildup that physically restricted airflow. Because your exhaust pipe is welded directly to the converter housing, visual inspection is impossible without disassembly. However, diagnostic logic can still point toward a failing unit even before tearing into the welds.

The most definitive non-invasive check involves monitoring the rear oxygen sensor (O2S) data stream via an OBD-II scanner. A healthy catalytic converter acts as a chemical buffer, smoothing out the rich and lean oscillations generated by the engine. When you view the live data graph of the downstream O2 sensor, it should display a relatively flat line or very low frequency switching once the vehicle reaches operating temperature. If the signal continues to switch rapidly between high and low voltage values after the upstream sensor has stabilized, the converter is failing to store oxygen effectively. This indicates the internal honeycomb structure is either collapsed or saturated with debris.

Another critical metric is the efficiency reading provided by modern ECU firmware. The engine control unit calculates a "Catalyst Efficiency" percentage based on the amplitude difference between the upstream and downstream O2 sensor signals. A reading consistently below 85% (or whatever threshold your specific ECU defines as a fault) confirms that the device is not converting pollutants at the required rate. While this doesn't always mean immediate failure, it suggests the unit is degrading and will likely fail an emissions inspection soon.

Physical temperature checks can also reveal issues. A clogged converter often runs significantly hotter than normal because of the increased friction and incomplete combustion occurring downstream of the restriction. If you have access to a thermal camera or can carefully feel the heat (with extreme caution), a hot spot localized at the converter rather than the exhaust tip is a strong indicator of flow restriction. Conversely, if the unit feels excessively cold to the touch while the vehicle is under heavy load, it may be so clogged that no gases are passing through, though this is rarer than overheating scenarios.

Replacing a welded-on converter like your G6's requires careful planning. If you cut into the welds to swap the unit, ensure you use high-quality welding techniques or a replacement part specifically designed for your VIN to avoid re-enacting the quality issues that prompted the recall in the first place. Always verify the replacement part's specifications against the original equipment manufacturer data to ensure it meets current emission standards without introducing new backpressure problems.

For those managing vehicle maintenance at scale, tracking catalyst efficiency trends over time can predict failures before they become critical power losses. Integrating OBD-II data logging into your fleet management system allows you to spot degradation patterns early, scheduling replacements during routine service rather than waiting for a breakdown. This proactive approach minimizes downtime and avoids the higher costs associated with emergency repairs on the road.
